text: # Lamina Lamina runs [Qwen3.8-Flash-Next](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next), a 125-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on one PC with NVIDIA GPUs and plenty of RAM, and [Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) and [Qwen3.8-27B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B) on one GPU or a few. It serves them through the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs and its own web app, for chat, coding agents and pictures. The experts live in RAM and run where it is fastest: the GPUs keep the ones the model uses most and the CPU computes the rest beside them. Each step decodes several tokens at once: a draft layer proposes them and one pass of the model checks them all, so the text is the model's own. How it works: [docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md](docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md). Lamina is a fork of [Strata](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata) by Niko1221 and its contributors. Since 2026-10-29 it follows its own course: NVIDIA GPUs only, extra GPUs as further expert tiers, and a draft layer trained on the engine's own output. Its speeds against llama.cpp and Strata on one PC are in [docs/COMPARISON.md](docs/COMPARISON.md). ## What you need - **An NVIDIA GPU** of compute capability 8.0 or newer (RTX 30, 40 or 50 series, or the workstation cards of those generations), with a driver for CUDA 13. The model runs on one GPU that nothing else uses: no display, no other program. Up to three more GPUs become further expert tiers, and these may drive the display. The engine is developed on an RTX 3090 (24 GB), with an RTX 5070 Ti (16 GB) and a second RTX 3090 as tiers. A smaller card holds fewer experts and runs slower. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B take more GPUs differently: their layers are split over the fewest that hold the whole model. Qwen3.8-27B, a dense model, needs ~36 GB of VRAM at its full context (262,144 tokens, K and V in 8 bits): two GPUs, such as a 24 GB and a 16 GB one. - **RAM** for the experts, which are pinned while the model runs: | Model file | RAM taken | Download | | --- | --- | --- | | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, [ISTA-DASLab's GSQ-RCO IQ3_S](https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF) | ~53 GB | ~86 GB | | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, [unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) | ~81 GB | ~114 GB | | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, [unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF) | ~22 GB on one GPU, ~2 GB split over GPUs that hold it | ~24 GB | | Qwen3.8-27B, [unsloth's UD-Q6_K_M](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF) | ~2 GB | ~24 GB | The engine also runs unsloth's other Flash-Next quants, all but UD-IQ1_S and BF16: UD-IQ1_M, UD-Q2_0, UD-IQ2_XS, UD-Q2_K_XL, UD-IQ3_XXS, UD-Q3_K_XL, UD-IQ4_XS, UD-Q5_K_XL, UD-Q6_K_XL and Q8_0, whose experts take ~35 GB (UD-IQ1_M) to ~128 GB (Q8_0) of RAM, and [Agention's Gyro-L](https://huggingface.co/agentionai/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-GGUF). Setup downloads none of them: [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md) says how to run one. The engine compares the experts with the PC's RAM before it loads them: it stops when they do not fit, and warns when little would be left. - **An SSD**: Flash-Next reads a 28.8 GB table of per-layer embeddings from the model file at every token. - **A 64-bit x86 CPU with AVX2** (AVX-512 is used when it is there), or a 64-bit Arm CPU with Armv8.2's dot product and FP16 instructions, where the experts run on ggml's dot products (built and its CPU tests run, not yet run with a GPU). The CPU computes the experts no GPU holds, so its cores and the RAM's bandwidth set much of the speed. - **Windows 10 / 11 or Linux**, and Python 3.10 or newer for setup. - **To build:** the CUDA toolkit 13.0 or newer, and Visual Studio 2022's C++ tools on Windows (their CMake and Ninja serve the build; on Arm also LLVM's clang-cl), or GCC, CMake 3.24 or newer and Ninja on Linux. The [releases](https://github.com/eddoursul/Lamina/releases) have the programs built for RTX 30, 40 and 50 GPUs. ## Install **A release:** extract both archives of a [release](https://github.com/eddoursul/Lamina/releases) for your platform into one folder: the programs (`lamina-server`, `lamina`, `lamina-vision`) and the CUDA runtime they load. Download a model's GGUF files into a folder of their own: one of the table's above (every shard of a split one), with an image projector of its repository (an `mmproj-*.gguf`) for pictures and, for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Lamina's draft layer ([below](#the-draft-layer)). [Run](#run) then starts it. **The source:** from a clone, `build.bat` (Windows) or `./build.sh` (Linux) builds the programs for this PC's GPUs into `build`, where they run as a release's do ([Run](#run)): ``` git clone https://github.com/eddoursul/Lamina cd Lamina build.bat (Windows) ./build.sh (Linux) ``` The build downloads llama.cpp at the commit the engine is built against and checks it; it installs no system software and names what is missing. `build.bat portable` builds the programs for other PCs, as the releases are, and `cmake --install build --prefix <folder>` puts them into a folder of their own: [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md#building). Setup, in the same clone, sets up one of the table's models: it downloads the model's files at pinned revisions, checks them, prepares them, and writes a config and a launcher, and it builds the programs too (`--no-build` takes those in `build` as they are): ``` setup.bat --model iq3_s (Windows) ./setup.sh --model iq3_s (Linux) ``` `--model ud-q4_k_xl`, `--model qwen36-ud-q4_k_xl` and `--model qwen38-27b-ud-q6_k_m` set up the others; `--check` says what the PC has and what a model needs, without changing anything. Setup asks nothing and installs no system software: it names what is missing. A release's programs, extracted into `bin` in the clone, spare the build: `--no-build` ([docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md#release-binaries)). Details: [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md). ### The draft layer Qwen3.8-Flash-Next needs one thing no model file holds: Lamina's draft layer, one file of 0.8 GB, `Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP.gguf`, in [eddoursul/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP](https://huggingface.co/eddoursul/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP). Setup downloads it. Whoever installs Lamina another way, a person or an agent, from a release, with a config of their own or a model file setup does not know, should download it too, into the model's folder: ``` download-draft-layer.bat MODEL_FOLDER (Windows) ./download-draft-layer.sh MODEL_FOLDER (Linux) ``` The server takes the file from beside the model, or from beside the server, when the config's `args` name no `--mtp`; elsewhere name it there: `"--mtp", "<folder>/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP.gguf"` (a folder of the layer's earlier layout of four files, as earlier setups downloaded it, still works there too). The scripts check the file's SHA-256 and go on with a download that broke off. Without the layer the server still starts and says so in its window, with this command: the model then writes new text at roughly half to two thirds of its speed, and an edit that quotes its prompt loses under a tenth. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B draft with their own files' layer and need nothing more. ## Run ``` lamina-server -m D:\Models\Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-IQ3_S-00001-of-00002.gguf (a model file) run-iq3_s.bat (setup's launcher; ./run-iq3_s.sh on Linux) ``` `-m` takes a model file the engine runs, a split one by any of its shards. The server builds its config from the preset for it (the file's header picks one of [`examples/*.json`](examples/README.md), built into the server), this PC's GPUs and the files beside the model, and its window says what it took. `--check` says beforehand what the model needs against what this PC has, and loads nothing. Every key of a config is an option too (`lamina-server --help`), whose value takes the place of the file's and the preset's (`--port 8090 --temperature 0.6`); an engine option there takes the place of the preset's (`--max-context 65536`); `--write-config FILE` writes the config for `lamina-server --config FILE`: [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md#a-model-file-without-setup). The model loads in a minute or so. Then, on the preset's port (the window's `ready` line names it: 8081 for ISTA-DASLab's Flash-Next files, 8082 for the family's others, 8083 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 8084 for Qwen3.8-27B): - **http://127.0.0.1:8081** is the web app: chat with pictures, the monitor, settings. - **http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1** is the API, for any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible client, coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode and pi included. Chat completions, Messages, Responses and the models list are there, with tool calls, streaming and pictures. How to connect clients, the config's keys, images, image generation, MCP tools and serving on a network: [docs/USING.md](docs/USING.md). ## A fixed chat template The server renders prompts with the chat template in the model's file. Lamina also carries [froggeric's fixed template for Qwen 3.5, 3.6 and 3.8](https://huggingface.co/froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates) (v22.5) in `data/chat-template-froggeric-v22.5.jinja`. To enable it, add this key to the model's config, `lamina-<model>.json`, and start the server again: ```json "chat_template_file": "data/chat-template-froggeric-v22.5.jinja" ``` A relative path starts at the config's `cwd`. The server's log then says `[lamina] chat template: ...data/chat-template-froggeric-v22.5.jinja`. Remove the key to go back to the model's own template. A conversation's history renders as it does under the model's template but for its system turn and the warnings below, and a cached conversation is read again once. It has been tested on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, on both model files. What it changes: - **The default effort.** A request that names no reasoning effort runs at `medium` instead of `xhigh`, with no effort sentence in the prompt, and thinks less. `high` still means `xhigh`. A config's `"reasoning_effort": "high"` keeps `xhigh` as the default. - **The tool instructions.** The system turn says more about how to call tools. # How Lamina works Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 125 billion parameters, but each token passes through a small part of them: most of the model is experts, and each token uses 10 of a layer's 512. Lamina keeps all of them in RAM, puts the ones the model uses most on the GPUs, computes the rest on the CPU beside the GPUs, and checks several tokens in each pass of the model. This page describes the parts; the options named here are in [SETUP.md](SETUP.md#engine-options), the measured speeds in [COMPARISON.md](COMPARISON.md). The figures were measured on the development PC with an RTX 3090 as the main GPU and an RTX 5070 Ti and an RTX 5060 Ti as tiers, Ryzen 7 9700X, DDR5-5600. ## The model - **48 layers**: 36 Gated DeltaNet layers, whose memory of the text is a fixed-size state, and 12 attention layers (every fourth), whose indexer scores the context and picks 2,048 of its tokens for each query to attend to. - **The residual stream** is four streams of 2,560 values (hyper-connections), which each layer reads and writes through small learned mixes. - **Experts**: each layer has 512 routed experts and a shared one. A router picks 10 routed experts for each token; the 48 layers hold 24,576 of them, about 47 GiB in IQ3_S and 72 GiB in UD-Q4_K_XL. - **Per-layer embeddings**: an extra input to the layers, from a table of 320 million rows (28.8 GB). Each token reads 16 of its rows, picked by hashes of the token and the two before it. - **An MTP layer**, trained with the model to predict the token after the next: Lamina's draft layer. ## Where the parts live - **The main GPU** runs everything each token passes through: the DeltaNet and attention layers, the hyper-connection mixes, the routers, the shared experts, the output head, the draft layer, the K/V cache of the attention layers and the DeltaNet states. The rest of its VRAM holds experts: on a 24 GB GPU about 9,200 of IQ3_S's, 5,600 of UD-Q4_K_XL's. - **Further GPUs** (`--second-gpu`) hold the next experts in line, about 6,300 and 7,500 of IQ3_S's on the two 16 GB tiers, and compute them in each pass beside the CPU. - **RAM** holds every expert, in one pinned block per layer that the GPUs can copy from. The CPU computes the experts no GPU holds, where they lie: a pool of worker threads, one per physical core but the one that drives the GPUs, with AVX2 or AVX-512 kernels (ggml's and the engine's own). - **The SSD** holds the per-layer embeddings. Each token's 16 rows are read past the OS file cache, as soon as the token is known, and arrive while the GPU runs the embedding and the first layer; rows read before stay in a small cache. On the development PC, with all three GPUs, 87-98% of the routed experts the tokens use are on a GPU (UD-Q4_K_XL on an edit 87%, IQ3_S on thinking text 98%); the CPU computes the rest, from under one to six experts a layer. ## Which experts the GPUs hold Routing is uneven: some experts serve far more tokens than others, and a conversation favours its own. The engine starts from a profile that ranks all 24,576 experts by how often the model routes to them (`data/expert-profile.bin`, built into the programs, or what this PC's runs learned: [SETUP.md](SETUP.md#the-config)); the main GPU takes the top of the list and each tier the next. While the model runs, the engine counts which experts the conversation routes to. Every round (`--adapt-every 1` in the configs) each GPU's adaptive tier ranks the counts, older ones decayed, and replaces its least-used experts with more-used ones it lacks, up to 96 an update. The copies go out while the GPU's link carries nothing else: between layers for the main GPU, between passes for the tiers. A tier counts an expert that a later tier holds at half its use, since moving it would only shift work from one GPU to another. The first tier also gets the next layer's likely experts ahead of time: on a side branch of each layer, the next layer's router runs on an estimate of its input, and while the RAM is idle the likeliest experts no GPU holds are copied to that tier, up to 12 MiB a layer (to a tier whose link moves 20 GB/s or more). ## Generating: verify windows Each step of generation is one pass of the whole model over a **verify window**: the last token and the drafts after it, up to 4 tokens in the configs (`--spec 4`), up to 8 with prompt lookup. Each window size is a CUDA graph, captured once. For each layer: 1. The main GPU runs the layer's mixer and its router, and writes the router's choices and the layer's input, in 8-bit form, to host memory that the CPU and the GPUs all reach. 2. The host splits the routed experts: those the main GPU holds, each tier's, and the rest for the CPU pool. 3. All of them compute at once: the main GPU its experts, each tier its share (its rows are copied over to the main GPU when they are done), the CPU pool the rest, writing its rows to host memory. 4. The main GPU waits for the others' rows, adds them to its own and goes on with the next layer. The main GPU waits for the host and the other devices by spinning on flags in host memory: its graph never stops, so the hand-offs cost microseconds. It is also why nothing else may use that GPU: a display or another program makes the driver share it in time slices, and a spin that loses its slice stalls the pass. A tier after the first gets only these short shares, and a driver may slow its card between them until its rows come late. `--second-gpu-clocks` locks a tier's clocks while the engine generates, `--second-gpu-clocks-hold` and `--second-gpu-clocks-lead` time that lock around a request, and `--second-gpu-sleep-us` lets such a tier sleep while the CPU pool would not need it: its experts go to the tiers before it and the CPU, its lock is released, and it comes back when the text turns heavy. Each is off unless a config sets it: the clocks are a card's own, and the sleep gives up speed for power by an amount that is the model file's and the PC's ([examples/](../examples/README.md)). After the last layer, the output head gives each token of the window its next-token distribution. The window's tokens are accepted from the first while each draft is the token the model picks there (greedy: the likeliest; sampled: the one drawn from the model's distribution), and the model's own token follows the last accepted draft. So a pass yields one token or several, and every token is the one the model itself picks at its position. A pass over several tokens takes far less time than as many passes over one: the weights are read once for all of them. ## Drafts - **The draft layer** is the model's MTP layer, run on the last token's final state and its own output: it proposes up to 3 tokens, each kept while its probability under the draft layer stays at 0.5 or more (`--spec-min-p 0.5`). Its experts are 2-bit, it attends to the last 32,768 tokens, and its head covers a fixed subset of 40,525 tokens of the vocabulary (it never drafts the others), scored through a 2-bit copy and the best ones again exactly. Its dense part was trained further on this engine's own output, so its drafts are right more often. It is one GGUF file of its own ([eddoursul/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP](https://huggingface.co/eddoursul/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP)): no model file holds it, and the server takes it from beside the model. - **A sampled request's drafts**: a position's token is drawn with a number that follows from the seed and the position alone, so the engine knows the number a draft will meet. The draft is still the layer's likeliest token, which passes when the model's likeliest token is the same and the number falls inside its share of the distribution; from the draft's probability, the number and the temperature the engine reckons that chance (`include/lamina/core/draft_pass.hpp`) and keeps the draft when it is at least what a draft at the floor has under an average number. A draft whose number has already lost it takes no place in the window, one a little under the floor stays when its number is small, and a greedy request keeps the plain floor. - **Prompt lookup**: where the last 16 tokens of the text occurred before (`--spec-lookup 16`), up to 7 of the tokens that followed them there take the drafts' place. An answer that quotes its prompt, such as a file returned with an edit, then passes about 7.5 tokens a step. On the development PC a greedy pass yields 2.0-2.4 tokens on thinking text, 3.8-4.1 on

# Using Lamina The server, `lamina-server`, runs the engine in its own process and serves the OpenAI, Anthropic and Responses APIs and a web app. The launchers setup writes start it with the model's config (`run-iq3_s.bat`, or from the clone's folder `build\lamina-server.exe --config lamina-iq3_s.json`). It listens on the config's `port` (setup's defaults: 8081 for IQ3_S, 8082 for UD-Q4_K_XL, 8083 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 8084 for Qwen3.8-27B; `--port` overrides it), on this PC only unless told otherwise ([below](#from-other-devices)). Ctrl+C in its window stops the engine, which saves its learned expert profile, and the server. ## The web app `http://127.0.0.1:8081/`: **Chat** (with pictures, the thinking level, MCP tools, chats kept in the browser), **Monitor** (what the engine is doing, the last requests, the GPUs, CPU and RAM) and **About** (the addresses to give clients, the settings). Its **Model settings** card changes a few settings for the running server and writes them into its config file ([below](#the-config)); only the page itself can change them. ## The API | | Endpoint | | --- | --- | | OpenAI Chat Completions (stream and non-stream, tools) | `POST /v1/chat/completions` | | Anthropic Messages (stream and non-stream, tools) | `POST /v1/messages`, `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` | | OpenAI Responses (stream and non-stream, tools; stateless, [below](#codex-cli-and-the-responses-api)) | `POST /v1/responses` | | A choice among single-token options in one pass, nothing generated ([below](#one-pass-choices)) | `POST /v1/choose` | | The model list, health | `GET /v1/models`, `GET /models`, `GET /health` | | The model's properties (llama-server's fields) | `GET /props` | | What the model is doing now | `GET /status`, `GET /slots` | | Everything the Monitor shows; Prometheus' format with vLLM's names on `Accept: text/plain` | `GET /metrics` | | Request totals in Prometheus' format under llama-server's names | `GET /metrics/prometheus` | | The MCP servers, their state and tools | `GET /mcp` | | The prompt a chat request is read as; a text's token ids and back (llama-server's fields) | `POST /apply-template`, `POST /tokenize`, `POST /detokenize` | | Image generation, when set up ([below](#image-generation)) | `POST /v1/images/generations` | | Unload the model now, or load it ahead of a request | `POST /unload`, `POST /load` | ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{ "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about GPUs."}], "max_tokens": 512}' ``` ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1", api_key="none") r = client.chat.completions.create(model="local", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]) print(r.choices[0].message.content) ``` Any model name is served; `/v1/models` lists the config's `model_name` and its `aliases`. An answer's `timings` use llama.cpp's names, with the drafts offered and accepted. Prometheus' scrape of `/metrics` carries vLLM's metric names (`vllm:num_requests_running`, the token and request counters, the draft counters, time to first token and between tokens), so dashboards written for vLLM read this server; the Monitor's other facts come under `lamina:` and their JSON key (`lamina:live_tok_s`, `lamina:gpu_util`, ...). Ready to use in [monitoring/](monitoring/): a Prometheus scrape config (`prometheus.yml`, the API key sent as a bearer token), a Prometheus Operator `ServiceMonitor` and a Grafana dashboard of both name sets (`grafana-lamina.json`). ## Clients - **Apps with an OpenAI-compatible provider**: base URL `http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1`, any API key (or the config's `api_key`). Zed's llama.cpp provider reads `/props` and offers tools from its `chat_template_caps`. - **Claude Code**: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8081`, `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` set to a Claude model name it knows (the server ignores the name), and any `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` (or the `api_key`). - **OpenCode**: a provider in `opencode.jsonc`, with the context setup chose: ```jsonc { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "provider": { "lamina": { "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible", "name": "Lamina", "options": { "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1", "apiKey": "none" }, "models": { "flash-next": { "name": "Qwen3.8-Flash-Next", "limit": { "context": 262144, "output": 32768 }, "options": { "reasoningEffort": "high" }, "variants": { "low": { "reasoningEffort": "low" }, "none": { "reasoningEffort": "none" } } } } } }, "model": "lamina/flash-next" } ``` OpenCode compacts the conversation before `limit.context`; keep `limit.output` well under it. - **Codex CLI**: [below](#codex-cli-and-the-responses-api). - **A terminal chat**: `.venv\Scripts\python.exe chat.py --port 8081` (`/image <path>` attaches a picture, `/think` sets the thinking level, `/reset` starts over). ## Thinking The model thinks before it answers (streamed as `reasoning_content`; Anthropic: `thinking` blocks). Choose how much per request: | API | | | --- | --- | | OpenAI | `"reasoning_effort": "none" \| "low" \| "medium" \| "high"` (also `"reasoning": {"effort": ...}`, or `"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}`) | | Anthropic | `"output_config": {"effort": "low" \| "medium" \| "high"}`, `"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}`, or `"thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}` (under 2K = low, under 8K = medium, more = high) | Without a setting the model uses its own default, high; `"reasoning_effort"` in the config sets another for requests that name none. The levels are instructions the model was trained with, not a token limit: - **A thinking budget**: `"reasoning_budget_tokens": N` in a request or the config caps the thinking at N tokens; the server then ends it with a short wrap-up and `</think>`, and the model answers from there (nothing is read again). - **The answer keeps its room**: with thinking on, no budget and a `max_tokens` of 1,024 or more, the thinking is wrapped up when a quarter of the cap (at least 512 tokens) is left; without `max_tokens`, at three quarters of the context. `"answer_room": false` in the config turns it off. - **`"effort_position": "end"`** in the config puts a non-default effort in a short system turn before the answer instead of the top of the prompt, so a request that only changes the effort reuses the cached conversation. - **`"anthropic_thinking": "on_request"`**: an Anthropic request that asks for no thinking gets none (Anthropic's rule; Claude Code's short helper calls want it). The default thinks as the model's template does. ## Sampling A request's `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `min_p`, `seed`, stop strings (`stop`; Anthropic `stop_sequences`) and penalties (`presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, `repetition_penalty` with `penalty_last_n`; llama.cpp's `repeat_penalty` and `repeat_last_n` too) are honored. The config's `sampling` block sets the defaults for requests that leave them out; what it leaves out comes from the model card's settings for the request's thinking state (thinking: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20; not thinking: temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20, presence_penalty 1.5). The example configs sample at temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0, presence_penalty 0. `"temperature": 0` decodes greedy. `top_k` keeps at most 64 candidates. Every token, drafted or not, is the model's own pick: with sampling, a draft is kept only when it equals the token the model sampled for its position, so the drafts change the speed, never the distribution. The expert tiers adapt to the conversation in the background, so a sampled answer is reproducible run to run only with `--adapt-every 0` in the engine's arguments. ## Behaviour - **Streaming**: with `"stream": true` the thinking, the answer and tool calls (name first, then the arguments piece by piece) arrive as they are made; a long prompt sends keep-alives so agents do not time out, and `"return_progress": true` sends llama.cpp's `prompt_progress` (total, cache, processed, time_ms) per prompt chunk instead. Closing the connection stops the model, so the next request starts at once. - **Tool calls** are taken out of the text when the request declares tools; without them the answer is the model's text as written. `"tool_call_recovery": true` in the config also reads calls the model writes in a few other forms (`<parameter=NAME>`, JSON inside `<tool_call>`, a bare `<function=NAME>` block). - **Context**: a request longer than the context is refused (400), never cut. One whose `max_tokens` would run past the context is answered with `max_tokens` shortened to the room left (agents ask for 32,000 on every request); `"fit_max_tokens": false` in the config (or `--no-fit-max-tokens`) gives llama.cpp's 400 instead. - **The prompt cache**: a request continues from the longest start of its prompt the engine holds, so the next turn of a chat or an agent reads only what is new. Each conversation keeps its own checkpoints of the sequence state in RAM (at each turn and in long prompts; `--prompt-cache N`, default 16 per conversation), and a conversation another request replaces (a chat app's title request, a subagent) is parked in RAM with its K/V and its checkpoints (`--conversation-cache-mib MIB`, default 16384; `--conversation-cache-slots N` caps their number, by default only the memory does) so switching back continues where it was. A parked conversation leaves only whole, the least recently used first; `--conversation-cache-min-tokens N` (default 1024) keeps shorter ones out. They never take the RAM below `--ram-reserve-mib MIB` (default 6144) available to the system, and leave between requests when it runs below it: the expert arena is pinned, so without it a park beside a large arena swaps the rest of the system instead (0: only the budget limits them). The Monitor's Conversation cache card shows them. The engine keeps the model's own token ids of each reply for the next turn. Responses report the reused tokens (`usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`; Anthropic: `cache_read_input_tokens`). - **Guards**: a reply that repeats one token 256 times ends as `"length"` (`"repeat_stop_tokens"` sets the run, 0 turns it off); a verify window whose logits are not finite emits nothing, the engine drops its cached state and the server retries the request once if nothing was sent yet. `"reasoning_close_retry": true`

# Setup What a PC needs: [the README](../README.md#what-you-need). This page covers the build from the source, what setup does, a model file run without it (`lamina-server -m`), the release binaries, the config, the GPUs, the engine options worth knowing, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B, and Docker. ## Building From a clone of this repository, with the CUDA toolkit 13.0 or newer and, on Windows, Visual Studio 2022's C++ tools (its free Build Tools with the workload "Desktop development with C++" do), on Linux GCC, CMake 3.24 or newer and Ninja (Ubuntu 22.04's CMake is 3.22: `pip install cmake` or Kitware's packages): ``` build.bat (Windows) ./build.sh (Linux) ``` They build the preset `native` of `CMakePresets.json` into `build/`: `lamina-server`, `lamina` and the image encoder `lamina-vision`, on Windows with the CUDA runtime's DLLs beside them (on Linux they take the toolkit's), for this PC's CPU and its GPUs of the RTX 30 series and newer, as `nvidia-smi` names them at each build (after a card is added, build again). The programs run from there: `build\lamina-server -m MODEL.gguf` ([below](#a-model-file-without-setup)). `build.bat portable` (`./build.sh portable`) builds them for other PCs into `build-portable/`, as the releases are: RTX 30, 40 and 50 GPUs (compute capability 8.6, 8.9 and 12.0, with PTX for newer ones), any x64 CPU with AVX2 or arm64 CPU with Armv8.2's dot product and FP16 instructions, the MSVC runtime linked in. CMake options after the preset's name go to its configure (`build.bat native -DLAMINA_BUILD_TESTS=ON`, `--fresh` for a new start of the build folder). The presets work with CMake alone too: `cmake --preset native`, `cmake --build --preset native` (on Windows in a Visual Studio developer prompt). - **llama.cpp**: the first configure downloads it at the commit the engine is built against, checks its SHA-256 and unpacks it into `third_party/llama.cpp`, without llama.cpp's web app (`tools/ui`, whose deep paths pass Windows' 260-character limit). `-DLAMINA_GGML_DIR=<folder>` names another checkout. - **The tools**: `build.bat` finds Visual Studio 2022 (else 2019 or 2026) itself, or takes a developer prompt's, and its CMake and Ninja unless the PATH has others; on Windows on Arm it compiles C and C++ with LLVM's clang-cl (Visual Studio's "C++ Clang Compiler for Windows" or LLVM's own: ggml's CPU code for Arm does not build with MSVC). nvcc is the one on the PATH, in `CUDA_PATH` or in `/usr/local/cuda`; `CUDACXX` names another, `CXX` the C++ compiler (on Linux nvcc's host compiler too: `CXX=g++-14` when the GCC is newer than the toolkit takes). - **The checks**: a CUDA toolkit older than 13.0 stops the configure (engines built with CUDA 12.8 crashed in long prompts on RTX 50 GPUs), as do 13.2.0 and 13.2.1 for RTX 50 GPUs (their nvcc compiled some of the kernels wrong: the answers were garbage), and GPUs older than the RTX 30 series are left out. - **Jobs**: half the logical cores compile and link at once, so that the PC stays usable, fewer when the free RAM holds fewer (1.5 GB a job: nvcc's largest files take up to 0.9 GB); `-DLAMINA_JOBS=N` sets another number. A build that stops is tried once more: CUDA's ptxas now and then fails to read a file it has just written. - **What it builds**: the three programs. `-DLAMINA_BUILD_TESTS=ON` adds the tests (`ctest --test-dir build`), the parity checks and the tools, which otherwise build by name (`cmake --build build --target verify_parity`); `-DLAMINA_BUILD_VISION=OFF` leaves the image encoder out. `cmake --install build --prefix <folder>` puts the programs into a folder of their own, flat, as a release's two downloads extract: the programs, `download-draft-layer.bat` (`.sh` on Linux) and the licenses (the component `lamina`), and the CUDA runtime and cuBLAS the programs load, with NVIDIA's license (`cudart`; `--component` installs one). Installed on Linux, the programs load the libraries in their own folder. ## Setup From a clone of this repository: ``` setup.bat --model iq3_s (Windows) ./setup.sh --model iq3_s (Linux) ``` `setup.bat` and `setup.sh` make a Python environment, `.venv` (setup takes the standard library only; a build's CMake and Ninja go into it), and run `setup.py` with the same arguments. The models: `iq3_s` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, ISTA-DASLab's GSQ-RCO IQ3_S), `ud-q4_k_xl` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL), `qwen36-ud-q4_k_xl` (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL) and `qwen38-27b-ud-q6_k_m` (Qwen3.8-27B, unsloth's UD-Q6_K_M). The engine also runs Flash-Next's other GGUF files, most of unsloth's quants and [Agention's Gyro-L](https://huggingface.co/agentionai/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-GGUF) among them: setup downloads none of those, so copy a config, name the file after `--native` and give it a port of its own ([COMPARISON.md](COMPARISON.md#gyro-l-and-the-three-files-at-one-build)). Of unsloth's Dynamic 3.1 quants it refuses UD-IQ1_S (a layer with its gate and up in two formats) and BF16, saying so at load. A quant's n-gram table can be one of unsloth's engram tables (BF16, Q8_0, Q5_1 or IQ4_NL): add `"--ple-gguf", "<the table's file>"` to the config's `args`, or rename the file over the quant's table shard as unsloth's README says. Without `--model`, setup builds the engine only. | Option | | | --- | --- | | `--check` | say what this PC has (GPUs, RAM, disk, the tools) and what the model needs; change nothing | | `--data-dir DIR` | where the model files go (default `../Lamina-data`, beside the clone) | | `--vision on\|off\|gpu[:GPU]` | pictures (default on; the image encoder runs on the CPU). `gpu` runs it on a GPU: the one named (name, UUID or nvidia-smi index), else the one with the least VRAM besides the main GPU, of those that drive no display if any; it takes ~1.3 GB there | | `--main-gpu GPU` | the GPU the model runs on (default: the one with the most VRAM that drives no display) | | `--context N` | the context in tokens (default: the example config's) | | `--port N` | the server's port (default 8081 to 8084 by model) | | `--update` | `git pull` this clone first | | `--no-build` | use the programs as they are: a release's in `bin/` ([Release binaries](#release-binaries)), else those already built | | `--cuda-archs A` | the CUDA architectures to build for, e.g. `86;120` (default: this PC's GPUs) | | `--portable` | build the engine for other PCs (any AVX2 CPU; arm64: Armv8.2 with dotprod and fp16), as the releases and the Docker image are | Setup asks nothing, installs no system software (it names what is missing) and moves or deletes no file. A step whose result is already there is skipped, so setup runs again after an interruption or for another model: 1. For a build, CMake and Ninja into `.venv` and llama.cpp at the commit the engine is built against, into `third_party/llama.cpp`: ggml for the engine, mtmd for the image encoder. With `--no-build` nothing. 2. The server with the engine, `build/lamina-server` (`.exe`, with the CUDA runtime DLLs beside it; `build/lamina` is the engine alone), for this PC's GPUs, and the image encoder, `build/lamina-vision`: llama.cpp's mtmd library with the model's projector, built with CUDA for the same GPUs in `build-vision-cuda` and copied beside the server, which starts the `lamina-vision` in its own folder (no config key names another). The config's `vision` section decides where it runs at each start: on the CPU beside the engine (`"gpu": false`, the default), where it hides the GPUs so they keep their VRAM for experts, or with `--vision gpu` on the GPU the option picks (`"gpu": true`, `cuda_device`). Its CPU code is built for any AVX2 CPU: a native build on an AVX-512 CPU loses flash attention and encodes about half as fast. 3. The model's files from Hugging Face at pinned revisions, into the data folder, resumed when interrupted and checked once by size and SHA-256 (`<file>.sha256` beside each records the check): [ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF), [unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF), [unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF) and [unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF). `HF_ENDPOINT` names a mirror. 4. Their preparation, for Flash-Next only: the MTP draft layer, `mtp/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP.gguf`, from [eddoursul/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP](https://huggingface.co/eddoursul/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP); with pictures, from the same repository the image projector in Q8_0 (ISTA-DASLab's BF16 one through `tools/mmproj_q8.py`), which the CPU encodes ~20% faster. Everything else comes from the GGUF files at start: the server reads the tokenizer and the chat template, the engine the experts, the projections and the float tensors (put in the forms it takes in memory, in milliseconds). Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8-27B with pictures use their repositories' projectors (`mmproj-F16.gguf`) as they are. 5. The config, `lamina-<model>.json`, and its launcher, `run-<model>.bat` (`run-<model>.sh` on Linux), from `examples/<model>.json` with this PC's GPUs and data folder. A config written before keeps the keys the example lacks (an `api_key`, an `images` section). **The draft layer without setup.** `download-draft-layer.bat FOLDER` (`./download-draft-layer.sh FOLDER` on Linux; a release's archive has its platform's script beside the programs) downloads step 4's file into a folder, at the same revision, checked by its SHA-256 and a broken download resumed. A config whose `args` name no `--mtp` takes `Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP.gguf` from beside the model, else from beside the server, and the server's window says which; elsewhere the `args` name it: `"--mtp", "<folder>/Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP.gguf"`. A folder of the layer's earlier layout (`dense.txt`, `dense.bin`, `experts.bin`, `draft_vocab.bin`), as earlier setups downloaded it to `mtp/rt-distilled`, still works as `--mtp`. # Troubleshooting The engine's log is the config's `log`, `lamina-<model>.log` in the clone's folder; the server writes to its window. `setup --check` says what the PC has and what a model needs. ## Building **"Visual Studio's C++ tools are needed".** `build.bat` found no Visual Studio 2022 (nor 2019 or 2026) with the C++ tools: install Visual Studio 2022 or its free Build Tools with the workload "Desktop development with C++", which has CMake and Ninja too, or run `build.bat` from a developer prompt of the one to use. **"CMake 3.24 or newer is needed", "Ninja is needed", or CMake's "CMake 3.24 or higher is required".** Install them: on Windows Visual Studio's "C++ CMake tools for Windows" (part of that workload) or cmake.org's; on Linux the distribution's `cmake` and `ninja-build` (Ubuntu 22.04's CMake is 3.22: `pip install cmake`). **"No CMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER could be found".** The CUDA toolkit is not installed, or its nvcc is neither on the PATH nor in `CUDA_PATH` or `/usr/local/cuda`: install the toolkit 13.0 or newer, or name its nvcc, `CUDACXX=<path to nvcc>`, and build with `--fresh` (`build.bat --fresh`), as the build folder keeps the first compiler it found. **"Lamina builds with the CUDA toolkit 13.0 or newer, and ... is 12.x".** Name a newer toolkit's nvcc with `CUDACXX` and build with `--fresh`. **"CUDA 13.2.0 or 13.2.1 compiles some of the engine's kernels wrong for RTX 50 GPUs".** The answers would be garbage: use CUDA 13.0, 13.1 or 13.2.2 and newer (`CUDACXX`, `--fresh`), or build for older GPUs only (`-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86`). **"CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES is native, and nvidia-smi names no NVIDIA GPU ...".** The NVIDIA driver is missing, or `nvidia-smi` is not on the PATH, or the GPUs are older than the RTX 30 series. For another PC's GPUs: `build.bat portable`, or name them (`-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86;120`, quoted for `build.bat`). **Linux: the build stops at `unsupported GNU version`.** The GCC is newer than the CUDA toolkit accepts. Install an older one beside it (g++-14) and name it: `CXX=g++-14 ./build.sh --fresh` (nvcc then takes it too; `CUDAHOSTCXX` names nvcc's alone). For setup: `CXX=g++-14 ./setup.sh ...`. **"llama.cpp ...: the download failed".** The build fetches llama.cpp from GitHub at its first configure: check the network (an HTTPS proxy is taken from `https_proxy`) and build again. **"... holds a llama.cpp this build did not download"**: `third_party/llama.cpp` is a copy of another origin; move it away, or name it with `-DLAMINA_GGML_DIR=<folder>`. ## Setup **"missing for the build: ...".** Setup installs no system software: install what it names (the CUDA toolkit 13.0 or newer; on Windows Visual Studio 2022's Build Tools with the workload "Desktop development with C++"; on Linux a C++ compiler, `build-essential` on Debian and Ubuntu), then run setup again. `LAMINA_NVCC=<path to nvcc>` and `LAMINA_VCVARS=<path to vcvars64.bat>` pick a toolkit and a Visual Studio when there are several. **"no NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 8.0 or newer ... was found by nvidia-smi".** The NVIDIA driver is missing, or `nvidia-smi` is not on the PATH, or the GPUs are older than the RTX 30 series, which Lamina does not run on. **Setup warns about CUDA 13.2.0 or 13.2.1.** Their compiler builds some of the engine's kernels wrong for RTX 50 GPUs (sm_120): the answers are garbage. Use CUDA 13.0, 13.1 or 13.2.2 and newer; `LAMINA_NVCC` picks one installed beside it. **A download broke off.** Run setup again: it goes on from where it stopped. **"... has the right size but not the pinned file's SHA-256", or "... bytes, not the pinned file's".** The file in the data folder is an older or damaged copy. Move it away and run setup again to download it. ## Starting **The PC is slow or stops responding for a minute or two while the model loads.** The engine reads the experts into RAM and locks them there for the GPUs (the server's window says when). Wait; the next starts are faster while the model file stays in the OS file cache. **"not enough RAM: the model's experts take ...".** The experts stay locked in RAM while the model runs (the README's table), and this PC's RAM cannot hold them beside the ~4 GiB the system needs. Use a smaller quant: IQ3_S takes ~28 GB less than UD-Q4_K_XL. With GPUs of ample VRAM, `--vram-pin-gib` keeps some experts there instead of in RAM. Qwen3.6's experts take RAM only when they do not all fit in VRAM: more GPUs (`--second-gpu`) or a shorter context avoid it. **"RAM is tight: ...", or the PC pages heavily.** The model fits, but less than 6 GiB of RAM would stay available beside it: other programs hold the rest, or the model leaves little. Windows pages them out to disk while the model runs, and Linux may end the engine. Close other programs, or use a smaller quant. **"...: not a model Lamina runs (its architecture '...'; ...)".** `-m` names a GGUF that is no model of these families: an image projector (`mmproj-*.gguf`), the draft layer, another model. Name the model's file, a split one's first shard or any other. **"--mmproj ...: the projector of a model N wide, and this one is M", or "... not an image projector".** The file `--mmproj` names belongs to another model, or is no projector: name the one of the model's repository, or leave `--mmproj` out and the server takes the one beside the model. **"unknown argument: ..." and "the engine of this model does not take an option of the command line (above)".** An option on `lamina-server`'s command line that is not the server's goes to the engine, whose parser refused it: a typo, a value it does not take, or an option of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's engine given for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B or Qwen3.8-27B (or the other way). `lamina --help` lists Flash-Next's options; [SETUP.md](SETUP.md#qwen36-35b-a3b-and-qwen38-27b) the qwen35 path's. **"the config's "..." is no key lamina-server reads (lamina-server --help lists them): ignored".** A key of the config file that no option names: a typo, or a key of another program or an earlier version. The server starts without it; `lamina-server --help` lists every key beside its option. **"the vision section (--vision-*) names no image projector".** Pictures were asked for (a `--vision-...` option, or a `vision` section in the config) and no projector names the model's: give one with `--mmproj FILE`, or turn pictures off with `--no-mmproj`. **"port N is already in use - is Lamina (or another server) already running?".** Another server listens on the config's port: close it, or start this one with `--port`. **"the config has a "vision" section, and the image encoder is not there: ...".** The server starts the `lamina-vision` (`.exe`) in its own folder and no other: a release has it there, and setup copies the one it builds there. Put it back (a release's programs archive extracted whole, or setup run again), or take the `vision` section and `"--vision"` out of the config to run without pictures. **"the vision encoder did not start: ERR this lamina-vision was built without CUDA ...".** The `lamina-vision` beside the server is a CPU-only build and the config's `vision` section asks for a GPU (`"gpu": true`). Set `"gpu"` to `false` (and remove `cuda_device`), or put the CUDA build back: a release's programs archive, or setup run again. **"the vision encoder did not start: ERR lamina-vision sees no GPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=...)".** The config's `vision` section asks for a GPU (`"gpu": true`) and the encoder sees none: its `cuda_device` names a card that is not in this PC (moved, replaced, or a config from another PC), or is not a UUID or number CUDA takes, or the driver gives no GPU. `nvidia-smi -L` lists the cards with their UUIDs: name one there, or set `"gpu"` to `false`. **"WARNING: no draft layer (...)".** Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's draft layer, `Lamina-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP.gguf`, is neither beside the model nor beside the server, or the config's `args` name a file that is not there (`"--mtp", "<file>"`), or a folder without the files of the layer's earlier layout (`dense.txt`, `dense.bin`, `experts.bin`). The server runs, and the model writes new text at roughly half to two thirds of its speed. Run the command the warning gives (`download-draft-layer.bat FOLDER`, `./download-draft-layer.sh FOLDER` on Linux: 0.8 GB), do what it adds about the config, and start the server again ([SETUP.md](SETUP.md#setup), The draft layer without setup). **"mtp: ... is not a draft layer this engine reads".** The file `--mtp` names is another GGUF (a model, a projector) or the draft layer of another format: download the layer again with the script. **"this build has no kernels for its compute capability, ...".** The engine was built for other GPUs: a card added after the build, or a release's programs on a card other than the RTX 30, 40 and 50 series. Build again from the source (`build.bat`, `./build.sh`, or setup): the build is for this PC's GPUs.
